items.stem: Describe the role of different religious groups in the development of anti-colonial feelings in Vietnam.
items.answer: Religion played an important part in building anti-colonial feeling in Vietnam. Vietnamese religious belief was a blend of Buddhism, Confucianism and local practices, so when the French introduced Christianity the Vietnamese reacted sharply and were angered by it. As a result an early anti-Christian movement, the Scholars' Revolt, broke out in 1868, led by officials of the Imperial Court who resented the spread of Christianity and of French power. The French suppressed the revolt, but the uprising inspired other patriots to rise against them; the Hoa Hao movement led by Huynh Phu So in the Mekong delta in 1939 was likewise significant in the growth of the anti-colonial movement.

items.stem: Describe the economic conditions of Britain after the 'First World War'.
items.answer: Britain, the leading economy of the pre-war world, went through a prolonged crisis after the First World War. To pay for war expenditure it had borrowed heavily from the United States, so the war ended with Britain carrying huge external debts. The war had also loosened its hold on the Indian market, where the nationalist movement had grown and anti-British feeling had spread among ordinary people, and where promoting Indian industry had become a nationalist aim, which hurt British industry. At home unemployment rose sharply while agricultural and industrial production fell; cotton production collapsed and cotton exports dropped dramatically. Unable to modernise, Britain found it hard to compete internationally with the United States, Germany and Japan.
items.concept: Economic impact of the First World War

items.stem: Briefly discuss the merits of globalisation and write three steps which have been taken by government to promote it in India.
items.answer: Merits of globalisation: it allows goods and services to flow freely across the world because trade barriers are reduced; it allows technology and experience to move freely between countries; it allows capital to flow freely among nations; and to some extent it allows labour to move to different countries. Steps taken by the Government of India to promote globalisation: trade barriers have been lifted since 1991 under a free trade policy adopted under pressure from the Ministerial Conference of the World Trade Organisation, an agency of the United Nations; technology and experience are being exchanged with several countries; restrictions on imports and exports have been minimised and taxes on imported goods reduced; and both central and state governments encourage investors from abroad to invest in India.

items.stem: Explain the causes of the Great Depression.
items.answer: The main causes of the Great Depression were the following. First, agricultural over-production: as farm prices and farm incomes fell, farmers tried to make up the loss by producing still more, which pushed prices down further and left produce rotting in the market for want of buyers, deepening their hardship. Second, the financial dependence of many countries on the United States: many countries had taken loans from the US, which were easy to raise while conditions were good, but by 1929 US overseas lenders panicked at the first sign of trouble and stopped lending to European countries, halting production there. Third, financial collapse: banks failed, currencies such as the British pound-sterling collapsed, and agricultural and raw material prices slumped, while the US government doubled import duties to protect its own economy, which dealt world trade another severe blow.

items.stem: What was the contribution of Christopher Columbus?
items.answer: Christopher Columbus discovered the vast continent that later came to be known as the Americas. With that discovery began cultural exchange with the original inhabitants of the continent. Foods such as potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes, unknown to people of other continents, were carried out of the Americas and became part of everyday diets elsewhere. From the sixteenth century the vast lands, abundant crops and minerals of America began to transform trade and lives everywhere, and precious metals, particularly silver from mines in present-day Peru and Mexico, enhanced Europe's wealth and financed its trade with Asia.

items.stem:
How did Silk Routes link the world ? Explain with three suitable examples.
or
Describe any three features of Silk Routes.
items.answer: The Silk Routes linked the world in the following ways. First, they are a good example of vibrant pre-modern trade and of cultural links between distant parts of the world. Second, the name 'Silk Routes' itself points to the importance of west-bound Chinese silk cargoes carried along the route. Third, historians have identified several silk routes, over land and by sea, which knitted together vast regions of Asia and linked Asia with Europe and northern Africa; they existed from before the Christian Era and thrived almost till the fifteenth century. Chinese pottery travelled the same routes, as did textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia, while in return precious metals, gold and silver, flowed from Europe to Asia.

items.stem: Describe three types of flows or movements identified by the economists. What were the effects of these flows ?
items.answer: Economists identify three types of flows within international economic exchanges: the flow of trade, which in the nineteenth century largely meant trade in goods; the flow of labour, that is the migration of people in search of employment; and the flow, or movement, of capital invested over short or long distances. The effects were far-reaching. All three flows were closely interwoven and affected people's lives more deeply than ever before. The interconnections could sometimes be broken, for example when restrictions were placed on the migration of labour while goods and capital moved more freely. Looking at the three flows together helps us understand the nineteenth-century world economy better.
items.concept: Three flows of the world economy

items.stem: Write a short note on Indian entrepreneurs settled abroad.
items.answer: Indian bankers and traders who settled abroad financed trade across the world. Bankers such as the Shikaripuri Shroffs and the Nattukottai Chettiars used their own funds or funds borrowed from bankers in European countries, and financed corporate offices and organisations in India as well as the export of agricultural produce from Central and Southeast Asia. Indian traders and moneylenders, such as the Hyderabadi traders, opened emporia and offices for bulk sale in almost every seaport of the colonies across Europe and Africa, where they sold local agricultural produce, handicrafts, curios and antiques.

items.stem: Enlist the reasons because of which need for new economic policy was felt in India. Also write its objectives.
items.answer: The reasons that prompted the need for a New Economic Policy were the increase in the fiscal deficit, the increase in the deficit on the balance of payments, the Gulf crisis, the fall in exchange reserves, the rise in prices, and the poor performance of public sector undertakings. Its main objectives were the liberalisation of the economy, dispensing with too many controls, the expansion of the private sector, the encouragement of private foreign investment, the modernisation of agriculture, and control of the fiscal deficit.

items.stem: What were the aspects of New Economic Policy adopted in India ?
items.answer: The New Economic Policy began a process of economic reform in July 1991, and its main thrust was the liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation of the economy. All industries except four were freed from licensing, the ceiling of ₹100 crore on maximum investment by a company was removed, and most restrictions on direct foreign investment were lifted. Limits on users of foreign exchange were liberalised, and as a step towards privatisation newer areas were opened to the private sector. Only five industries remained reserved for the public sector, and as a step towards globalisation domestic industry was exposed to competition from multinational companies, with imports of capital goods and technology allowed.

items.stem: What are the monetary reforms under the New Economic Policy ?
items.answer: Under the New Economic Policy several monetary steps were taken on the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee: the direct credit programme was abolished, interest rates were freely determined, the banking system was reconstituted, banks were given more freedom, the accounting system was improved, and the liquidity ratio was reduced.

items.stem: Discuss the positive aspects of globalisation and liberalisation.
items.answer: Globalisation and liberalisation brought several positive results. They helped bring about rapid economic development, creating a large industrial base and increasing industrial production. The proportion of people living below the poverty line was reduced, self-sufficiency in food was achieved, and savings were mobilised. Resources for development were generated, a large pool of scientists and technically skilled persons was formed, and export-oriented units were established.

items.stem: What were the main sources of attraction for Europeans to come to Africa in the late nineteenth century ? How did they exploit their resources ?
items.answer: Europeans were drawn to Africa in the late nineteenth century by its vast resources of land and minerals. They came hoping to establish plantations and mines that would produce crops and minerals for export to Europe. To get the labour these needed, inheritance laws were changed so that peasants were displaced from the land, only one member of a family being allowed to inherit it, with the result that the others were pushed into the labour market. The Europeans also divided the different regions of Africa among themselves.
items.concept: Rinderpest and colonial control in Africa

items.stem: Explain the role of technology in shaping the world economy of the 19th century.
items.answer: Technology shaped the nineteenth-century world economy in three main ways. First, through changes in transport and communication: railways, steam shipping and the telegraph were inventions without which the transformation of the nineteenth-century world cannot be imagined. Second, by linking the various markets of the world: new investment and improvement in transport, faster railways, lighter wagons and larger ships moved food more cheaply and quickly from distant farms to final markets. Third, through its impact on the meat trade: until the 1870s meat was shipped from America to Europe as live animals that were slaughtered on arrival, which took up much ship space, and many animals died in the voyage, fell ill, lost weight or became unfit to eat, so meat prices were high and beyond the reach of the European poor and demand and production stayed low; the invention of refrigerated ships made it possible to carry meat itself from one region to another.
items.concept: Three flows of the world economy

items.stem: Discuss the darker side of expanding international trade and globalisation in late 19th century.
items.answer: Trade flourished and markets expanded in the late nineteenth century, but this was not only a period of expanding trade and growing prosperity; it had a darker side. First, loss of freedom and livelihood: in many parts of the world the expansion of trade and the closer relationship with the world economy also meant the loss of people's freedoms and livelihoods. Second, the division of Africa among imperialist powers: in 1885 the big European powers met in Berlin to complete the carving up of Africa between them. Third, the rise of colonial powers at the cost of colonised peoples: Britain and France made vast additions to their overseas territories in the late nineteenth century, and Belgium, Germany and the United States also became colonial powers.
items.concept: Rinderpest and colonial control in Africa

items.stem: What is Group 77 ? Why did Group 77 countries demand a New International Economic Order? Explain.
items.answer: The Group of 77 is a group of 77 developing countries that organised themselves as a separate bloc in order to share in the benefits of the fast growth the western economies experienced in the twenty to twenty-five years after the Second World War. They demanded a New International Economic Order for these reasons: to gain real control over their own natural resources; to obtain more development assistance from the advanced western countries; to secure better and fairer prices for their raw materials; and to win better access for their manufactured goods in the markets of the developed countries.

items.stem: Explain the impact of the First World War on Britain.
items.answer: Post-war economic recovery proved difficult for Britain because the heavy expenditure on the First World War had weakened the British economy. While Britain was preoccupied with the war, industries developed in Japan and India, so Britain now had to face competition from these countries, especially from Japan. To finance war expenditure Britain had borrowed liberally from the United States, which meant that at the end of the war it was burdened with huge external debts. The war had also brought an economic boom, that is a large increase in demand, production, prices and employment; when the war boom ended production contracted and unemployment increased.
items.concept: Economic impact of the First World War

items.stem: Why was there a need for clearing lands in Britain during the 19th century ? Explain any three reasons.
items.answer: Land tracts were cleared in Britain for several reasons, of which three are important. First, the increasing demand for food-grains: Britain's population grew very fast in the late phase of the eighteenth century, so the demand for food-grains rose, and land was cleared to expand the area of farming and meet the need for eatables, food-grains, vegetables and fruit. Second, the introduction and expansion of the railways: it was not enough merely to clear land for agriculture, since railways were needed to link the agricultural regions to the ports, so land was cleared to lay new railway lines. Third, homes and settlements: people had to settle on the land in order to bring it under cultivation, and this meant building homes and settlements.
items.concept: Three flows of the world economy

items.stem:
Describe the effects of the Great Depression of 1929 on the United States of America.
or
'The US was severely affected by the Great Depression of 1929.' Justify the statement with examples.
items.answer: The United States was greatly affected by the Great Depression of 1929. With the fall in prices, US banks slashed domestic lending and called back loans. Many houses and businesses collapsed. Faced with falling incomes, many households could not repay their loans and had to give up their houses, cars and other consumer durables. Unemployment soared and people trudged long distances looking for work. Unable to recover their investments and loans or to repay depositors, thousands of banks went bankrupt and were forced to close: by 1933 over 4,000 banks had closed and 110,000 companies had collapsed.
